It provides a reasonable guideline upon which the level of indemnification implied by the phrase “reasonable and proper costs” may be measured under the Rules.
However, we refrain from defining with any precision the level of indemnification required in any given case.
All we say is that the level of indemnification must be both meaningful and reasonable.
The court's discretion to move up or down from that level having regard to the factors set forth in Rule 10.33 or in Rule 10.2(1) remains intact.

Rather, it is one of a number of tools that a trial judge may use in order to make a cost award which provides appropriate indemnification.

(b) as a mechanism or method by which a reasonable and proper costs award may be arrived at (i.e. a costs award pursuant to Schedule C or “a multiple, proportion or fraction of an amount set out in any column … of Schedule C).

Expenses of this kind are in fact a fee component and must be charged to the client as fees, although they may be itemized separately under the fees heading on an account.
The amount claimed by the Defendant for facsimile charges is not a proper disbursement.
It reflects an internal charge made by the firm to its clients as a part of its fee structure.
While it may be appropriate in that context, it is not a proper disbursement in a party and party taxation.
Transcripts In Millott Estate v.
Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 2002 CarswellAlta 1551, 322 A.R.
307, 9 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 292, Fraser J. allowed the costs of transcripts, and made the following comments at p.
326: The cost of transcripts was disallowed by McMahon, J., in S.G.H. v.
Gorsline (2001), 292 A.R.
329 (Q.B.), and by McDonald, J., in Reese et al. v.
Alberta (Minister of Forestry, Lands and Wildlife) et al.
In the latter case the comment was made that a party was served by second counsel (who could take notes).
In Sidorsky et al. v.
CFCN Communications Ltd. et al.
181 (Q.B.), the cost was allowed in reliance upon Nova, An Alberta Corp. v.
Guelph Engineering Co.
The latter allowed transcript costs because of the length of the trial (about one year) and the technical nature of much of the evidence.
It is clear that the transcripts were used by both parties in preparing arguments.
Further, the adoption by the Court of a new recording system for evidence made it uncertain that accurate transcripts could be obtained later if required.
For a combination of these reasons the cost of the transcripts is allowed.
In Mar Automobile Holdings Ltd. v.
Rawlusyk, 2001 ABQB 516, 93 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 141, Clarke J. disallowed a cancellation fee paid in respect of trial transcripts.
This decision may now be of doubtful value.
Second Counsel The relevant factors to be considered when determining if costs for second counsel should be granted were set out in 1242311 Alberta Ltd. v.
Tricon Developments Inc., 2020 ABQB 678, 2020 CarswellAlta 2062, 16 Alta.
L.R.

(7th) 120, in which Justice Gates said: [18] In support if its contention that second counsel fees are appropriate in this instance, the Defendant relies on the decision of Verville J in Cornelson[Cornelson v.
Alliance Pipeline Ltd.
In that instance, the court awarded full second counsel costs following trial.
As such, the court referred to, and relied upon, the decision in Chapell v Canadian Pacific Railway, 2011 ABQB 74.

In that case, the court reviewed the applicable principles in the following terms: Although the complexity of the issues and the general importance of the issues are important factors, the litigation need not be either complex or weighty for second counsel fees to be awarded: Kassam v Dragish
(1991), 1991 CanLII 13058 (AB QB), 123 AR 161 (Alta QB) at para 13.
However, in Alberta, monetary value of the case is a weighty factor: Kassam at para.

While second counsel need not be present at every court appearance, such counsel must assist in the preparation leading up to the presentation of the matter and such involvement must be justified by the nature of the case: Davidson v Patten, 2005 ABQB 521, 381 A.R.
6 (Alta QB) var'd on other grounds 2008 ABCA 65 (Alta CA) at para 19.
The amount claimed in second counsel fees is also a pertinent factor: Kassam at para 17.

In Kassam, at para 14, Veit J also suggested that courts should err, if at all, on the side of generosity by allowing the second counsel fee since party and party costs provide a check and balance by reimbursing only a fraction of the cost of second counsel at trial.

The Alberta Court of Appeal also came to a similar conclusion., that is, in a case of real doubt, erring on the side of the party which retained the second counsel: Viridian Inc. v Dresser Canada Inc., 1998 ABCA 275 (Alta CA) at para [19] In Alberta Mortgage[Alberta Mortgage & Housing Corp. v.
Strathmore Investments Ltd.
286 (Alta C.A.)], the Court of Appeal declined to order second counsel costs “in the absence of established need based on complexity of issues or law”: at para 2.

In Bruen, Shelley J awarded second counsel costs in a case she described as “only moderately complex”, but that “the case was an important one for both parties, given the substantial damages sought and the potential consequences of recognizing a novel duty of care”: at para 53.

She offered the following guidance in terms of the appropriate factors to be taken into consideration in determining the appropriateness of a second counsel fee: Courts have used the following factors to determine the appropriateness of second counsel fees:
(i) the general importance of the issue(s)
(ii) the value of the case
(iii) the complexity and scope of the issues
(iv) the size of the trial record
(v) the manner in which opposing counsel conducts the case; and
(vi) whether second counsel addressed the court.

While the Court in Clancy expressed a reluctance to award second counsel costs outside of cases involving complex issues or law, courts in other instances have suggested that they should err, if at all, on the side of generosity by allowing second counsel fees.

Courts will generally award second counsel fees where the issues at trial were complex, the damages sought were substantial, the second counsel actively participated at trial, and the party was not merely splitting work between counsel that could reasonably have been completed by one counsel alone.
In Hanke v.
Resurfice Corp., 2006 ABCA 116, 2006 CarswellAlta 417, 384 A.R.
52, 58 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 14, the Court said, at p.
16: This Court has expressed its reluctance to award second counsel costs “in the absence of established need based on complexity of issues or law”: Alberta Mortgage & Housing Corp. v.
Strathmore Investments Ltd.
286 (Alta.
C.A.) at para.
This Court has been prepared to grant second counsel costs where the other side's arguments were “extremely complex, puzzling, and far-ranging”: Watts v.
Wakerich, 2001 ABCA 207 (Alta.
Though not “puzzling”, the Respondents' arguments were necessarily of an order of complexity to properly address the multifarious and complex factual underpinnings.
The Appellant, accordingly, is entitled to second counsel fees.
One should err on the side of generosity in allowing second counsel fees.
In Alberta, the money value of a case is a weighty factor in determining if second counsel fee should be allowed.

In addition, the trial judge should consider not only the complexity of the trial issues, but also all other factors which, in a specific case, are relevant to the issue of what is a “reasonable and proper” charge for barristers and solicitors: rule 600(1)(a)(i).

It may be that the conduct of the other parties in the matter of additional counsel is an indication of how complex those parties considered the trial issues; this comparison will not, however, be relevant in all situations.
In my view, the case does not have to be exceptionally complex or weighty before a second counsel fee is awarded.
It appears to me that the court should err if at all on the side of generosity in allowing second counsel fees since party and party costs provide their own form of check and balance in this matter.

Party and party costs will result in reimbursement for only a fraction of the cost of having a second counsel at trial; therefore, most parties will probably consider carefully whether they wish to bear that expense.
Kassam v.
Dragish (1991), 123 A.R.
161 (Q.B.), at 164, per Veit J.

With respect to motor vehicle accident trials, Montgomery J. said: In my judgment there are very few motor vehicle accident cases which warrant a second counsel fee because they are neither unusual nor complex, despite the effort of actuaries and economists to give an impression of complexity.
In my judgment, their reports and their evidence lack precision and conciseness.
Furthermore, the assessment of general damages is relatively easy, following the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Andrews v.
Grand and Toy (Alberta) Ltd.[citation omitted] and the other two cases.
Ropchan v.
Duncan (1992), 134 A.R.
Travel Costs of Out-of-Town Counsel In Hansraj v.
Ao (2002), 4 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 147 (Q.B.); additional reasons at [2003] 9 W.W.R.
236 (Alta.
Q.B.), Slatter J., at pp.
L.R.], discussed when travel costs for out of town counsel should be awarded: There are a few cases where the travel expenses of counsel have been allowed.
Some proceed on the assumption that the counsel retained had some special ability that could not be found in the judicial district in question: North American Systemshops v.
In others there were special reasons for the travel: Ligate v.
Abick (1991), 5 O.R.
(3d) 209 (trial moved due to limited court facilities); Reese v.
R.
450, 5 Alta.
R.
127 (counsel attended applications in Calgary, on an Edmonton action); Madgett v.
Dawley (1986), 170 A.R.
351 (multiple parties prevented retaining local counsel).

Apart from these exceptional cases, the general rule should be that travel costs for counsel to attend court proceedings in the judicial district where the action was started are not taxable. … It is undoubtedly true that parties have the right to select counsel of their choice.
However, that is not the issue; the issue is who is to pay for that choice.

Where counsel are retained outside the judicial district where the action is commenced, the travel expenses of that counsel are not taxable unless the party who retained out-of-town counsel can demonstrate that there were no competent counsel within the judicial district who could handle the matter, or other special reasons.
It is generally not sufficient that the party has formed a particular relationship with the counsel, or prefers for personal reasons to deal with that counsel.
Those are legitimate personal reasons to hire that counsel, but not sufficient reasons to pass the costs on to another party.
There was nothing unusual about this litigation.
I am not satisfied that the Defendants' insurer could not have retained counsel in Edmonton who could deal with these issues.
Accordingly, the travel expenses of counsel are not a proper disbursement.
The above statement was specifically approved by the Court of Appeal in Allen (Next Friend of) v.
University Hospitals Board, 2006 ABCA 101, 2006 CarswellAlta 412, 384 A.R.
23, 59 Alta.
L.R.
In Refco Alberta Inc. v.
Nipsco Energy Services Inc., 2003 ABCA 125, 2003 CarswellAlta 527, 327 A.R.
345, Wittmann J.A., at p.
348, made the following comments about paying the travel costs of out-of-town legal counsel: Charan Holdings Ltd. et al. v.
Mohawk Oil Co. et al., [1997] A.R.
Uned.

345 (C.A.), is a Memorandum of Judgment delivered from the Bench of this court and the disbursement issue for Calgary counsel travelling to Edmonton is dealt with simply by McFadyen, J.A., speaking for the court, indicating that, at paragraph [8]: As there is a transportation problem involved in this particular case, we will let you have the costs of the factum, but not the costs of travel to and from the city.
That is a matter you undertake in acting for your client and we do not think that should be visited on the opposite party.
In contrast to these authorities, Veit, J., in Waterous Investments Inc. v.
Liberton Holdings Ltd.

229 (Q.B.), did allow costs of the plaintiff's Calgary counsel travelling to Edmonton. … Waterous seems to be slightly at odds with the proposition that one is to embark on a notional hunt for “competent” counsel in Calgary in this case.
The competency of counsel must be viewed with some deference through the eyes of the client.
Trust and confidence must surround competence in a healthy and sustainable solicitor-client relationship.
Wittmann J.A. awarded the travel costs sought but indicated that he was “influenced by the amount requested” ($500.00) which he found to be reasonable (pp.
In Allen (Next Friend of) v.
University Hospitals Board, 2006 ABCA 101, 2006 CarswellAlta 412, 384 A.R.
23, 59 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 1, the Court of Appeal noted the comment that “trust and confidence must surround competence…”, and said, at p.
5: It does not follow, however, that a relationship so described is sufficient to merit an award of travel costs: Charan Holdings Ltd. v.
Mohawk Oil Co., [1997] A.J.
No.
1274 (Alta.
C.A.) at para.
The issue is whether, absent unique or exceptional circumstances, the additional expenses should be borne by the opposite party.
We think not. … 14.
Counsel's Out of Town Meals In Rendek v.
Dufresne (2006), 414 A.R.
371 (Alta.
Q.B.), Burrows J. held that meals for counsel who have travelled to the trial location are taxable costs.
At p.

377, his Lordship said: 26 Counsel's Out of Town Meals Fourth, the Plaintiffs included the cost of meals taken by Plaintiffs' counsel (who reside in Calgary) while attending the portion of this trial which was held in Edmonton.

At the request of the Defendants and in order to accommodate the Defendants and some witnesses the Defendants called, the judge who conducted the pre-trial conference in this Calgary action ordered that the Defendants' case be heard in Edmonton.
The Defendants say that Plaintiffs' counsel's meal costs would have been incurred wherever the trial was held and should therefore not be taxable.

27 The cost of meals taken when a lawyer is working out of town is usually paid by the client even though the lawyer is saving the cost of food he or she would have consumed (and not charged his or her client for) if he had been at home.
(The same goes, I observe, for judges travelling for out of town judicial assignments.

Her Majesty paid for my meals during the portion of this trial which was held in Calgary.) 28 It seems to be an accepted convention that the full cost of the meals is reimbursed to the traveller though in fact the traveller is saved the expense of meals which would otherwise have been taken without reimbursement at home.
The Plaintiffs will be expected to pay for their counsel's meals.
They should recover that expense.
The item is taxable.
Computer Research Charges already Included in Fees In Sidorsky v.
CFCN Communications Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 296 (Q.B.), the successful defendant claimed $2,960.69 in computer research charges as a disbursement.
McMahon J. disallowed the claim.
At p.
304, his Lordship said: Effectively this claim represents a portion of the cost of legal research and should therefore be considered a part of the fees taxed and recovered.

Whether counsel chooses to have the research undertaken manually or electronically is a matter of counsel's own choice depending upon questions of economics, technology available and arrangements with the client.
It is not a matter for taxation as a disbursement.
This portion of the learned trial judge's decision was not disturbed on appeal (see (1997) 53 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 255 (C.A.); reconsideration refused (1998) 216 A.R.
In Lalli v.
Chawla (1997), 53 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 121 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Johnstone agreed with McMahon J.
At p.
130, she said: In Warshawski v.
Argentia Beach (Summer Village) (1990), 106 A.R.
222 (Alta.
C.A.), the Court held: However, the real question is whether the computer searching by law is a disbursement of the sort described in Rule 600.
In our view it is ususally more akin to legal research or other work by a lawyer.
The question therefore is not whether the work was done in-house or contracted out.
The question is whether the allowance for legal fees in the costs otherwise taxable is adequate.
Schedule ‘C’ presumably contemplates some research.

If a party wishes to submit that the amounts in Schedule ‘C’ would not be adequate for any reason, including the extent or difficulty of the legal research involved, he can always make that submission.
We have not heard such a submission here.
In our view neither the problems before the Court, nor the contents of either factum, nor the contents of the oral argument on either side, suggests any special award of fees.
(at pp.

222–223) Similarly in this case, the oral submission of Plaintiff's counsel does not give me any reason to depart from the generally accepted view that computer research is a mechanical substitute for a lawyer's time spent in preparing for trial to which Schedule “C” is deemed to apply.
That is not to say that in appropriate circumstances it would not be an appropriate disbursement.
However, something more must be demonstrated to justify its award.
Veit J. applied Lalli v.
Chawla (1997), 53 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 121 (Q.B.), in Atkinson v.
McGregor (1998), 227 A.R.
376 at p.
In Pauli v.
Ace Ina Insurance, [2003] 11 W.W.R.
74 (Q.B.), Rooke J. said, at p.
98: Under Schedule C, one is entitled to costs for each step taken.
Often there is legal briefing required.
Before electronic research, legal briefing was manual, but there were no additional costs associated with it.
Since the technological advances to provide electronic research, prudent counsel have obviously gone to same, but the principle is the same: it is not a matter compensated.
See V.A.H. at para.
88; Reid v.
Stein et al.
90, § 56, Johnstone, J.
(Q.B.); Strandquist et al. v.
Coneco Equipment et al., [2000] A.R.
Uned.
86, 2000 ABCA 138, § 7; and Westline Oilfield Construction Ltd. v.
Petromet Resources Ltd. et al.
Costs related to e-discovery (database management of litigation records) In PM&C Specialist Contractors Inc. v.
Horton CBI Limited, 2018 ABQB 842, 2018 CarswellAlta 2282, Justice Michalyshyn had before him an application for additional security for costs.
The defendant applied for “$557,195 as further security for disbursements incurred and to be incurred relating to the electronic production and management of documents (hereafter ‘e-discovery’)”.

His Lordship ordered the posting of an additional $165,000, and said: [11] PM&C argues that the task of e-discovery should be considered part of the cost of litigation and thus not recoverable as a disbursement.

In turn, HCBI correctly notes that in the initial security for costs decision I concluded that that there is some authority for the award of disbursements for database management of litigation records.

The authorities include the following now provided by the applicant: Murphy Oil Canada Ltd v Predator Corp, 2005 ABQB 134 (CanLII), mentioning “imaging” of some 21,580 pages or records—a small fraction of the volume of e-discovery in the case before me.

And though McMahon J does not detail the expense approved as a recoverable disbursement, at para 38 he endorsed the use of e-discovery as: … prudent and undoubtedly saved all of the parties time and money.
Litigants should be encouraged to take steps that will reduce trial time greatly.
Cost recovery serves as such encouragement.
In my view costs of this nature are reasonable in preparing for trial in litigation of this magnitude.
Also see: J.S. v.
Clement [1995] O.J.
No.
Ct.

Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co v 2421593 Canada Inc, 2016 ONSC 6487 (CanLII), approving a $4,158 disbursement for an e-document data base described as charges by a law clerk and litigation support—sounds like law firm staff and the claim was allowed with a commentary that it is the sort of claim that should be encouraged

S(J) v Clement, 1995 CarswellOnt 2962, authorizing the reasonable expense of scanning documents, OCR of documents, costs of related software for managing the documents—all reasonable costs “of preparing for trial in a computerized era” (at para 15)

Harris v Leikin Group Inc, 2011 ONSC 5474 (CanLII), 2011 CarswellOnt 9491, allowing an $30,373.36 expense for electronic document production, an expense that was billed by counsel and not a third-party service provider (at para 34) and not opposed by counsel opposite (at para 35)
Justice D.M.

Brown in Harris engaged in a thoughtful analysis at paras 36–44 of the Ontario Civil Procedure Rules and the Sedona Canada Principles Addressing Electronic Discovery 2008 CanLIIDocs 1; he commented that, inter alia, the Sedona Canada Principles should not be regarded as mere suggestions to counsel, but as indicating to counsel that the expectations, obligations, requirements and procedures contained within those principles now form part of Ontario's Rules of Civil Procedure.
(I pause to note that the Sedona Canada Principles do not appear squarely to have attracted the attention of any published Alberta decision, the exception being Holtby, Re, 2011 ABASC 622 (CanLII).
That may be because they are accounted for within Alberta's Practice Note 4.
In any event, the Sedona Canada Principles have attracted considerable attention in Ontario (eg, Palmerston Grain, A Partnership et al. v.
Royal Bank of Canada, 2014 ONSC 5134 (CanLII), amongst may other cases) and to a more limited extent Manitoba (eg, Commonwealth Marketing Group Ltd. et al. v.
The Manitoba Securities Commission et al., 2008 MBQB 319 (CanLII)), New Brunswick (eg, ICS State v Irving Oil Limited, 2011 NBQB 141 (CanLII)), British Columbia (eg, Liquor Barn Income Fund v.
Mather, 2011 BCSC 618 (CanLII), amongst other cases) and Newfoundland (eg, GRI Simulations Inc. v.
Oceaneering International Inc., 2010 NLTD 85 (CanLII)).

A recent Working Group Report for the Uniform Law Conference of Canada, entitled Electronic Document Rules (August 14, 2018), describes the uptake of the Sedona Canada Principles in the courts and in certain provinces' rules of civil procedure: online at http://www.euclid.ca/Pub/Electronic_Document_Rules&newline;_ULCC_2018.pdf.) Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Ltd, 2011 ABQB 175 (CanLII), in which at para 29 security for costs was ordered, a component of which was a $600,000 claim for an electronic database and full fees associating with maintaining and updating it; contrary to the erroneous written submissions on behalf of HCBI, the court in Attila Dogan did not “order a flat fee of $600,000 for creating, updating and maintaining the database”.
In no sense did the court sanction or approve of the quantum of that claim.

In fact, and unfortunately, there is no way of knowing what part of the $1.6 million in security that was ordered in Attila Dogan was made up of the e-discovery claim. … [13] I conclude then on this application much as before, that there is some authority in Alberta and elsewhere in favour of recoverable third-party disbursements for e-discovery.
This decision adds to it.
No authority squarely against it was brought to my attention.
(The issue of recoverable law firm disbursements for e-discovery, though addressed favourably in Harris v Leikin Group Inc, above, does not arise in this case.)

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.31:2 Charges for experts See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. 1. General Principles The Rules provide that the unsuccessful party will pay the reasonable costs of experts' reports. A first thing to note about these provisions is that they do not interfere with the contractual relationship between experts and the party who hired them. In other words, the party who hires experts must pay the contractual cost of obtaining their opinion, except in the unlikely situation where the arrangement between the party hiring the expert and the expert is that the expert would be paid what the court considered to be a reasonable fee. One result of the distinction that must be made between the relationship between the party who hires the expert and the loser who must pay all or part of an expert report is that the expert is not entitled to be represented on the costs hearing related to the expert's fees since the expert's fees will be paid in their entirety by the party who hired them. A second thing to note about these provisions is that the court may determine that the cost of a given report should not be fully paid by the losing party even though the expert's report was useful in advancing the winning party's position. In other words, while a totally useless report which never should have been commissioned will not be required to be paid for by the party opposite, the fact that the court does not require a party opposite to pay the full cost of an expert's report does not necessarily cast any doubt on the value of that report. A third thing to note about experts' reports is the relationship that they bear to lawyers' fees. A winning party to litigation is not usually repaid all of its lawyer's fees; the losing party will only be required to pay a portion of the winning party's lawyer's fees. The amount of lawyer's fees that the losing party will be required to pay is a standardized amount for standardized services; these standardized fees and services are set out in Schedule C to the Rules of Court. The lawyer hired by the winning party may well charge more than the tariff, or charge for services that are not included in the tariff. The reason that the losing party is not required to pay all of the legal fees incurred by the winning party is for social policy: the cost of access to justice might be too high if all of a lawyer's fees to the winning side had to be paid by the losing side. Similar considerations relating to the cost of access to justice must motivate the assessment of reasonbleness of experts' fees. A fourth thing to note about experts' reports is that such reports are required in much litigation where the tendency of the court would perhaps be to make erroneous findings of fact about liability or loss without the assistance of such reports. The court should assess the reasonableness of obtaining the report not from the perspective of trial but from the perspective of the party at the time the expert report was commissioned. If getting the report was reasonable at the time, then the fact that the report was not useful at trial, or was not relied on at trial, or was not accepted at trial, is presumably not a factor that will determine whether the report should be paid for by the parties opposite. A fifth thing to note about the assessment of the cost of experts' reports is that the court's approach should be generous, reminding itself that litigants must make decisions about the retention of experts well before they have completed all trial preparations. Anderson v. Ball (1997), 214 A.R. 332 (Q.B.), at 333–34, per Veit J. In Seidel v. Kerr (2004), 27 Alta. L.R. (4th) 227 (C.A.), Wittmann J.A. said, at p. 230: … The primary factor in allowing expert witness costs is whether, at the time it was incurred, the expenditure was reasonable: Nova, an Alberta Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co. (1988), 89 A.R. 363 (Q.B.). 2. Categories of Experts There are two categories of experts: In any event, it is my further view that the subrule provides examples of two separate categories of experts whose charges are included in the term “costs”. The first category relates to charges of experts for attendance to give evidence at the trial. The second category, if the court so directs, relates to the charges of experts for investigations and inquiries or assisting in the conduct of the trial. I arrive at this interpretation on the basis that the words “such persons” as used in the subrule refer back generally to the persons listed, namely, “accountants, engineers, medical practitioners or other experts”. I could see some merit to the argument of the plaintiff that the subrule relates only to experts who attended to give evidence at the trial if the word “who” was used in place of the word “for” where it first appears in the subrule. As the rule stands, however, the argument of the plaintiff cannot prevail. Nova, An Alberta Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co. (1988), 60 Alta. L.R. (2d) 366 at 375 (Q.B.). In Sidorsky v. CFCN Communications Ltd. (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 296 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice McMahon dealt with, inter alia, the matter of private investigators fees as a disbursement. The plaintiff had sued a Calgary television station for defamation. He claimed damages in excess of $15.7 million. The defendant was successful at trial and sought investigator's fees in the amount of $252,751.32. His Lordship awarded a disbursement of approximately $200,000 for investigators' fees. The Court of Appeal [(1997), 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 255 (C.A.); reconsideration refused (1998), 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1999), 232 A.R. 189 (C.A.)], allowed an appeal from that award. At p. 270, the Court said: That investigatory fee related in large part to keeping track of witnesses and their changes of address… We must emphasize the definition of “costs” in Rule 600(1)(a), “all the reasonable and proper expenses”. In justifying the disbursement, the witnesses were identified as people who were transient and difficult to locate. In this case, it is unknown how many of these witnesses were transient, unwilling, or failed to notify the respondents of any change of address. A $200,000 award represents a significant sum. While judges must often, for practicable purposes, award disbursements on the basis of counsel's representations, when the award is of this magnitude it should not be awarded without evidence as to its necessity and reasonableness. As with costs generally, a notice to admit facts could have resolved this problem. Had the appellants failed to admit the facts involving these witnesses (which were later proven), the respondents would have been entitled to seek reimbursement for the costs of producing the witnesses, including some reasonable sum for keeping track of their whereabouts where that was required. However, no notice to admit was served. Frequently, keeping a list of the current addresses of witnesses is simply part of the overhead of a law firm and should not be the subject of a separate disbursement. As such, it should be included as part of the party and party costs award. The respondents then unsuccessfully applied for a re-hearing before the Court of Appeal [(1998), 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.)]. In Monashee Petroleums Ltd. v. Pan Cana Resources Ltd. (1988), 85 A.R. 183 (C.A.), Mr. Justice Côté at pp. 192–93, made the following observations about awarding costs in respect of experts retained for, but not called at trial: The plaintiff complains that the defendant's party-and-party costs at trial included a fee for an expert who did not testify. The defendant in his factum says that was less than a quarter of the fees charged by that expert. The defendant's expert was apparently held in readiness to rebut the plaintiff's expert who (in the event) only testified subject to objections by the defendant and the learned trial judge's deferring his ruling on the plaintiff's expert's admissibility until judgment. After lengthy cross-examination of the plaintiff's expert, counsel for the defendant did not call his rebuttal expert, possibly correctly divining that the learned trial judge would exclude the evidence of the plaintiff's expert. It has always been the rule that expenditures for witnesses are based on what seemed reasonable at the time, not on hindsight about witnesses who in the event turned out later to be unnecessary. Cost are for proper expenses, and expenses are incurred by ordinary mortals, not by prophets. The trial judge is in a much better position to assess that sort of a situation than an appellate court, and an award of one quarter is modest enough that I see no reason whatever to interfere with what (by rule 601) is a matter of discretion. In Hetu v. Traff (1999), 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 326 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Johnstone, at pp. 331 and 333, gave the following summary of the law: The law is clear that in determining whether an expert witness fee should be allowed, the test is whether the expenditure was reasonable at the time that it was made … Further, the successful party can receive costs for witnesses that were reasonably retained, regardless of whether or not those witnesses testify at trial. . . . . . … professionals that are not qualified as experts can nonetheless be awarded higher fees than that generally allowed for ordinary witnesses when they testify as to the professional services they rendered. 3. Costs Incurred Prior to Commencement of Action In Kha v. General Principles The Rules provide that the unsuccessful party will pay the reasonable costs of experts' reports.
A first thing to note about these provisions is that they do not interfere with the contractual relationship between experts and the party who hired them.

In other words, the party who hires experts must pay the contractual cost of obtaining their opinion, except in the unlikely situation where the arrangement between the party hiring the expert and the expert is that the expert would be paid what the court considered to be a reasonable fee.

One result of the distinction that must be made between the relationship between the party who hires the expert and the loser who must pay all or part of an expert report is that the expert is not entitled to be represented on the costs hearing related to the expert's fees since the expert's fees will be paid in their entirety by the party who hired them.

A second thing to note about these provisions is that the court may determine that the cost of a given report should not be fully paid by the losing party even though the expert's report was useful in advancing the winning party's position.

In other words, while a totally useless report which never should have been commissioned will not be required to be paid for by the party opposite, the fact that the court does not require a party opposite to pay the full cost of an expert's report does not necessarily cast any doubt on the value of that report.
A third thing to note about experts' reports is the relationship that they bear to lawyers' fees.
A winning party to litigation is not usually repaid all of its lawyer's fees; the losing party will only be required to pay a portion of the winning party's lawyer's fees.

The amount of lawyer's fees that the losing party will be required to pay is a standardized amount for standardized services; these standardized fees and services are set out in Schedule C to the Rules of Court.
The lawyer hired by the winning party may well charge more than the tariff, or charge for services that are not included in the tariff.

The reason that the losing party is not required to pay all of the legal fees incurred by the winning party is for social policy: the cost of access to justice might be too high if all of a lawyer's fees to the winning side had to be paid by the losing side.
Similar considerations relating to the cost of access to justice must motivate the assessment of reasonbleness of experts' fees.

A fourth thing to note about experts' reports is that such reports are required in much litigation where the tendency of the court would perhaps be to make erroneous findings of fact about liability or loss without the assistance of such reports.
The court should assess the reasonableness of obtaining the report not from the perspective of trial but from the perspective of the party at the time the expert report was commissioned.

If getting the report was reasonable at the time, then the fact that the report was not useful at trial, or was not relied on at trial, or was not accepted at trial, is presumably not a factor that will determine whether the report should be paid for by the parties opposite.

A fifth thing to note about the assessment of the cost of experts' reports is that the court's approach should be generous, reminding itself that litigants must make decisions about the retention of experts well before they have completed all trial preparations.
